analysis.one_liner: Restores tariffs on imported steel that President Bush had just removed.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: the Senate referred it to the Finance Committee on the day it was introduced, and it died there when the 108th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: In March 2002, President Bush put tariffs of up to 30% on imported steel to protect American steel mills. In December 2003 he ended them early, about a year and a half before they were set to expire. This bill, introduced days later by three Democratic senators from steel states, would have overridden the President and put the tariffs back in place until their original expiration date. It was sent to the Senate Finance Committee and never came out; the tariffs stayed gone.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would be workers and shareholders at domestic steel mills, and steel-producing towns in states like West Virginia, Indiana, and Pennsylvania, where jobs depend on keeping cheaper imported steel out of the market. Higher steel prices would have supported employment and profits at those mills, and the United Steelworkers union had been the policy's strongest backer in 2002. Steel-importing businesses and consumers would be the losers, since tariff costs get passed into the prices of cars, appliances, construction, and anything else made with steel.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would have brought back the tariffs on imported steel that President Bush imposed in March 2002 under Proclamation 7529, restoring the price protection those tariffs gave domestic steel mills.
It would have erased the December 4, 2003 proclamation that ended the tariffs, keeping the safeguards in place through their originally scheduled end date rather than a year and a half.
By introducing it, Sens. Byrd, Bayh, and Rockefeller put Congress on record against the President's decision, giving steel-state legislators a position to defend the jobs in their districts.

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, millions of American businesses and households would pay through higher prices for anything containing steel — autos, appliances, machinery, and construction. Studies of the 2002 tariffs found the costs to steel-consuming industries and consumers far exceeded the wages saved in steel jobs, and many more Americans work making things out of steel than making the steel itself. Trading partners also would have faced continued retaliation risk, as the 2002 tariffs had drawn European sanctions on American goods.

drawbacks.text: Tariffs on imported steel raise costs for the far larger number of Americans employed in steel-using industries — car makers, appliance makers, construction — and raise prices for consumers; the President removed the safeguards for exactly these reasons.

Safeguard tariffs are paid by American importers and passed on to American buyers, so the bill's cost is spread across millions of households and downstream manufacturers to protect one concentrated industry.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit would go to a narrow group: steelworkers and steel-producing communities in a handful of states, whose jobs and local economies depend on tariff protection [S2]. The cost would fall on everyone else — a few dollars per person spread invisibly across the price of cars, appliances, and construction, but adding up to more than the wages saved [S3]. For a bill with 3 sponsors and no committee action, the tradeoff was never seriously weighed on the record; it was a statement of support for steel country more than a live legislative effort.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced, and with the President's removal of the tariffs already a done deal, nobody brought it up again before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: On December 9, 2003, five days after the President's proclamation ended the steel tariffs, Sens. Byrd, Bayh, and Rockefeller introduced S. 1997 to bring those tariffs back through the end of their originally scheduled period.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; that was the last action ever taken on it.
The Finance Committee never held a hearing or a vote, and the Senate never considered the bill again before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005, so it died without a floor vote.
The result was that the steel safeguards stayed lifted, as the President had decided, and Congress never acted to reverse it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Steel-consuming industries and consumers are better off, because the tariffs that would have raised their costs never came back. The President's decision stood unchallenged by any law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Steel users and consumers; tariffs stayed gone

for.name: Sen. Robert C. Byrd
for.what_they_did: Introduced S. 1997 on December 9, 2003, to reinstate the steel tariffs the President had removed, and spoke for it on introduction.

for.name: Sen. Jay Rockefeller
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor of the bill.

for.name: Sen. Evan Bayh
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor of the bill.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearing, no markup, no vote — during the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: President George W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Had already lifted the steel safeguards by proclamation on December 4, 2003, and the bill was written specifically to reverse that decision; he could have vetoed it had it passed.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors were Democrats from steel-producing states, and the President whose action the bill would reverse was a Republican; no Republicans backed the bill in the record.

industries.note: Reinstated tariffs would keep cheaper imported steel out, protecting mill jobs and profits in steel-producing states. Most of the industry, however, could buy steel imports freely again after December 2003, since the bill never passed.
Higher steel prices raise their input costs and their prices to consumers, and can cost jobs in industries that employ far more people than steelmaking does.

industries.industry: Steel-importing firms and foreign steel exporters
industries.note: The tariff is paid at the border by importers and built into prices; foreign exporters lose access to the U.S. market while it is in force.

industries.industry: Consumers and businesses buying anything made with steel
industries.note: Tariff costs are passed through to prices of cars, appliances, and construction, spreading a small extra cost across nearly every household.
